title: modern gurus and their cautions (Keeper-framed)
hook: devotion to the guru as to God, or follow only his good deeds? two texts, two answers
tomorrow: a poet dies, and two communities claim him. then what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, modern gurus and their cautions handed the seeker viveka: clear sight, not suspicion. Today, the block's last day, and an honest argument.

One friend is all in on her coach: whatever he says, she does, and she says it's changed her life. Another takes the advice she likes and quietly skips the rest, and she says that's just being smart. Each thinks the other has it wrong. Hindu texts carry a version of that same argument about the guru, and both sides have scripture behind them. So today, no verdict. Let both speak.
screen: `ALL IN, OR PICK AND CHOOSE?` → `BOTH SIDES HAVE SCRIPTURE.` → `LET BOTH SPEAK.`

segments.voice: The first voice is the last verse of the Shvetashvatara Upanishad. In paraphrase: these teachings shine for the great-souled one who has the highest devotion to God, and the same devotion to the guru as to God. Here is that side's best case. Some things aren't learned like facts. They pass through trust, the way a young musician learns a raga by giving herself to a master, not by arguing every note. Some lineages treat the guru as a living doorway to God, and this verse is part of why. The second voice is a graduation speech. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends his students home. Speak the truth, he says. Practice dharma. Then, in paraphrase: whatever deeds of ours are good, follow those, and not the others. If you're ever in doubt, look to people who are thoughtful, devoted to dharma and not harsh. That side's best case: even a great teacher is a person, and sorting protects both the student and the teaching. The Gita leans in near its end, when Krishna tells Arjuna, in paraphrase: reflect on this fully, then do as you choose. Both voices are Hindu. Some readers hold them together: deep devotion, kept tied to dharma. The texts leave the argument open, and so does this lesson.
screen: `DEVOTION TO THE GURU AS TO GOD.` · `FOLLOW OUR GOOD DEEDS, NOT THE OTHERS.` · `REFLECT, THEN DO AS YOU CHOOSE.` · then, large: `TWO HINDU VOICES.`

segments.voice: Press your palms together at your chest, the namaste gesture of honor, and hold it for a few breaths. Then let your hands open and rest palms up on your knees, free to receive and free to choose. Move slowly between the two a few times, and notice that both can belong to one person.
Modern gurus and their cautions. Two old answers: devotion to the guru as to God, and follow only the good deeds.

howItsDone: Hindu traditions honor the guru deeply, and some lineages treat the guru as a doorway to God; the Taittiriya Upanishad's farewell (speak the truth, practice dharma, follow our good deeds) is also taught as guidance for students leaving their teachers.

chat.meaning: The Shvetashvatara asks devotion to the guru as to God; the Taittiriya's teacher says follow only our good deeds. Both are Hindu voices.

Shvetashvatara.meaning: an Upanishad whose last verse speaks of devotion to the guru

Taittiriya.meaning: an Upanishad with a teacher's farewell to his students

dharma.meaning: right action; the way things ought to go

raga.meaning: a melodic framework in Indian classical music

namaste.meaning: a greeting of honor, palms pressed together

sources.ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 6.23 (these teachings shine for the great-souled one who has highest devotion to God, and to the guru as to God)
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 (speak the truth, practice dharma; follow those of our deeds that are good, not the others; in doubt, look to the thoughtful, devoted and gentle)
Bhagavad Gita 18.63 (reflect on this fully, then do as you choose)
